subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 68-year-old man with chronic hypertension presents with palpitations. His pulse is irregularly irregular, and an ECG shows absent P waves with an irregularly irregular rhythm. Inspection of the neck veins shows a jugular venous tracing in which the usual deflection just before the x descent is not seen, while the c, x, v, and y components that follow are otherwise preserved.
question: Which of the following best explains this patient's jugular venous pressure tracing?

options.text: A prominent y descent that deepens with inspiration, due to restricted early diastolic filling
Absence of the presystolic deflection, because organized atrial contraction is lost
A single large fused systolic wave, because regurgitant flow obliterates the x descent
Loss of the early diastolic downstroke, because pericardial pressure prevents atrial emptying
Irregularly occurring large presystolic waves, because atrial contraction occurs against a closed tricuspid valve

explanation_correct: The a wave of the jugular venous pulse is produced by right atrial contraction and normally precedes the x descent. In atrial fibrillation there is no coordinated atrial systole, so the a waves disappear from the JVP tracing; the remaining components (c, x, v, y) are preserved. The irregularly irregular pulse and absence of P waves on ECG confirm the diagnosis.

explanation_incorrect.A: A prominent y descent that deepens with inspiration (Kussmaul sign) is characteristic of constrictive pericarditis, not atrial fibrillation; this patient's tracing lacks the a wave instead.
explanation_incorrect.C: A single fused c-v wave with loss of the x descent is the tracing of tricuspid regurgitation, in which systolic regurgitation into the right atrium raises venous pressure throughout systole.
explanation_incorrect.D: Loss of the y descent occurs in cardiac tamponade, when elevated pericardial pressure prevents early diastolic emptying of the right atrium; atrial fibrillation spares the y descent.
explanation_incorrect.E: Cannon a waves are seen in complete heart block or other AV dissociation, when the atrium contracts intermittently against a closed tricuspid valve; in atrial fibrillation organized atrial contraction is absent, so cannon a waves do not occur.

educationalObjective: Atrial fibrillation abolishes the a waves of the JVP because there is no coordinated right atrial contraction.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 54-year-old woman with a history of intravenous drug use presents with 3 days of fever. Blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus. Auscultation shows a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that becomes louder with inspiration. Her jugular venous pulse tracing shows a single large positive wave during systole, with the normal downward deflection between the c and v waves no longer discernible.
question: Which of the following best explains the appearance of this patient's jugular venous waveform?

options.text: Loss of right atrial compliance from chronic volume overload, producing giant a waves in late diastole
Impaired early diastolic emptying of the right atrium by a constricted pericardium, producing a deep y descent
Disorganized atrial electrical activity eliminating presystolic filling, eliminating all venous pulsations
Systolic backflow of blood into the right atrium across an incompetent valve, producing a fused c-v wave and loss of the x descent
Pulsatile transmission of aortic pressure through the venous system, producing a bisferious venous contour

explanation_correct: This patient has tricuspid regurgitation from infective endocarditis (classic in intravenous drug users), with the murmur louder on inspiration because inspiration increases venous return to the right heart. In tricuspid regurgitation, regurgitant systolic flow into the right atrium keeps right atrial pressure elevated throughout systole, so the x descent is abolished and the c and v waves merge into a single large c-v wave on the JVP tracing.

explanation_incorrect.A: Giant a waves reflect right atrial contraction against increased resistance and occur in tricuspid stenosis or right ventricular hypertrophy; they are a late diastolic finding, whereas this tracing shows an abnormal systolic wave.
explanation_incorrect.B: A deep, prominent y descent with a pericardial knock describes constrictive pericarditis; that abnormality is in early diastole, not a systolic fused wave.
explanation_incorrect.C: Atrial fibrillation abolishes the a wave but does not eliminate venous pulsations; this patient's murmur and fused systolic wave point to tricuspid regurgitation instead.
explanation_incorrect.E: Venous pressure is a right atrial pressure signal; it does not reproduce an aortic bisferiens contour, which is a feature of severe aortic regurgitation on arterial palpation.

educationalObjective: Tricuspid regurgitation replaces the normal x descent with a fused c-v wave on the JVP because regurgitant systolic flow raises right atrial pressure throughout systole.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 62-year-old man reports progressive dyspnea and abdominal fullness. On examination his jugular venous pressure rises with inspiration, a diastolic sound occurs shortly after S2, and his venous tracing shows a deep downward deflection immediately after the second heart sound, with the pressure rapidly returning to an elevated plateau. Cardiac MRI shows a thickened pericardium.
question: Which of the following best distinguishes this patient's jugular venous tracing from that of cardiac tamponade?

options.text: This patient has a prominent y descent from rapid early diastolic filling that abruptly stops, whereas tamponade abolishes the y descent
This patient has absent a waves from atrial fibrillation, whereas tamponade preserves all venous components
This patient has a fused c-v wave from systolic regurgitation, whereas tamponade preserves the x descent
This patient has absent x and y descents from uniformly elevated pericardial pressure, whereas tamponade shows both descents
This patient has a rising venous pressure during inspiration, whereas tamponade shows a venous fall with inspiration

explanation_correct: This patient has constrictive pericarditis: Kussmaul sign (JVP rising with inspiration), a pericardial knock, thickened pericardium, and a JVP with a prominent y descent producing the 'dip-and-plateau' (square root) contour. In constriction the pericardium permits rapid early diastolic filling that then abruptly halts, generating the deep y descent. In cardiac tamponade, high pericardial pressure holds right atrial pressure elevated throughout diastole, so early diastolic emptying is prevented and the y descent is absent.

explanation_incorrect.B: Absent a waves indicate atrial fibrillation, not constrictive pericarditis; constriction typically preserves atrial contraction and both descents except for the exaggerated y.
explanation_incorrect.C: A fused c-v wave with loss of the x descent is the signature of tricuspid regurgitation, which is unrelated to this pericardial process.
explanation_incorrect.D: Absent x and y descents do not describe constriction; constriction characteristically shows a prominent y descent, and the x descent is also preserved.
explanation_incorrect.E: The venous pressure rises with inspiration (Kussmaul sign) in this patient, but in tamponade the venous pulse also does not show the normal inspiratory fall; the distinguishing feature here is the prominent y descent, not the inspiratory direction.

educationalObjective: Constrictive pericarditis shows a prominent y descent (dip and plateau) on the JVP, while cardiac tamponade abolishes the y descent.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 45-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer develops worsening dyspnea and lightheadedness. Blood pressure is 86/64 mm Hg with a fall of more than 10 mm Hg in systolic pressure during inspiration, heart sounds are distant, and the jugular venous pulse is elevated. Her venous tracing shows a normal inspiratory pattern of the early systolic downstroke, but no downward deflection is seen in early diastole.
question: Which of the following best explains this patient's jugular venous pressure findings?

options.text: Loss of coordinated atrial contraction eliminates presystolic venous filling waves
Rapid, unimpeded early diastolic filling followed by abrupt halt creates a deep diastolic downstroke
Systolic regurgitation into the right atrium merges the c and v waves into one systolic plateau
Intermittent atrial contraction against a closed tricuspid valve creates irregular large presystolic waves
Elevated pericardial pressure prevents early diastolic right atrial emptying, eliminating the y descent

explanation_correct: This patient has cardiac tamponade from a malignant pericardial effusion: hypotension, pulsus paradoxus (a >10 mm Hg inspiratory fall in systolic pressure), distant heart sounds, and elevated JVP. The hallmark of the tamponade JVP tracing is an absent y wave: the high pericardial pressure keeps right atrial pressure elevated during early diastole, so the atrium cannot rapidly empty and the usual y descent is abolished. The x descent is typically preserved.

explanation_incorrect.A: Loss of a waves is the JVP finding in atrial fibrillation; this patient's tamponade does not abolish atrial contraction, and the described defect is in diastole, not presystole.
explanation_incorrect.B: A deep early diastolic downstroke (prominent y descent) is characteristic of constrictive pericarditis, the classic contrast to tamponade.
explanation_incorrect.C: A fused c-v wave with loss of the x descent describes tricuspid regurgitation; this patient's systolic downstroke is preserved.
explanation_incorrect.D: Irregular cannon a waves occur with AV dissociation such as complete heart block, not with pericardial tamponade.

educationalObjective: Cardiac tamponade abolishes the y descent of the JVP because elevated pericardial pressure prevents early diastolic emptying of the right atrium.
